present.explain: A Spanish verb changes its ending for who does it. For verbs like tomar: tomo (I), tomas (you), toma (he, she, you polite), tomamos (we). For verbs like comer: como, comes, come, comemos. Some common verbs change more: tengo, tienes, tiene; quiero, quieres, quiere. English mostly adds -s for he and she; Spanish has a different ending for each person.
present.why: The ending carries the person. [[Tomo]] already means I drink, and [[tomas]] already means you drink, so the ending is the part to listen for: [[Ella toma]] té y [[yo tomo]] café.

examples.text: Mi mamá toma café con leche.
examples.means: My mom drinks coffee with milk.
examples.literal: My mom drinks coffee with milk.

examples.text: Él tiene café y yo tengo té.
examples.means: He has coffee, and I have tea.
examples.literal: He has coffee and I have tea.

contrasts.says: Because the ending already says who, Spanish usually leaves out yo, tú and the rest.
After querer or poder the second verb keeps its basic form: quiero tomar, never quiero tomo.

mistakes.why: With yo the ending is -o.
For one person who isn't you or I, the ending is -a (or -e).

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

no-subject.explain: Spanish usually leaves out the word for who does it, because the verb's ending already says it: Tomo café is I drink coffee. Say yo, tú, él, ella or nosotros when it matters who, to contrast two people or to make clear who you mean: Tú tomas café y yo tomo té.
no-subject.why: English needs I or you in every sentence; in Spanish the ending does that job, so [[Tomo]] café is complete. Adding yo where nothing contrasts sounds like stressing I: [[Yo]] tomo café, me, not you.

examples.text: Tú tomas café y yo tomo té.
examples.means: You drink coffee, and I drink tea.
examples.literal: You drink coffee and I drink tea.

contrasts.says: The ending is what tells you who: tomo is I, tomas is you, toma is he or she.
English can't drop I or you; Spanish usually does.

mistakes.wrong: Yo tomo café, yo como bien.
mistakes.why: Repeating yo with nothing to contrast sounds heavy; the endings already say who.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every Spanish noun is either an el word or a la word, and the words with it follow: el teléfono, un libro; la mesa, una llave. Many el words end in -o and many la words in -a, but not all (el café, la leche), so learn each noun with its el or la. A few la words that start with a stressed a take el and un in the singular: el agua, un agua.
gender.why: The noun decides, and the little words around it agree. Change the noun and [[el]] becomes [[la]], [[un]] becomes [[una]], [[mucho]] becomes [[mucha]]: mucho café, mucha agua.

examples.text: El teléfono está en la mesa.
examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.text: Un té con leche, por favor.

examples.means: I drink a lot of water.
examples.literal: I drink a lot of water.

contrasts.says: English has one the and one a for every noun; Spanish has el or la, un or una, by the noun.
mi and tu are the same for el and la words: mi libro, mi llave.

mistakes.why: teléfono is an el word: learn it as el teléfono.
llave is a la word; learn it as la llave.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: A written question opens with an upside-down ¿ and closes with ?. A yes-or-no question can keep the order of a statement and just rise in tone: ¿El carro está aquí? After a question word like dónde, qué or cómo, the verb comes next, and the subject after it: ¿Dónde está el carro? Spanish never adds a word like English do.
question.why: The ¿ warns you a question is coming, so you hear it from the start. With a question word, the verb follows straight away: [[¿Dónde está]] el carro?, not ¿Dónde el carro está?

examples.means: What do you want to do?

contrasts.says: English adds do or does to most questions; Spanish doesn't, and puts the verb right after a question word.

mistakes.why: After dónde, the verb comes next.
A written question opens with ¿.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

ser-estar.explain: Spanish has two verbs for to be. estar says where something or someone is (El libro está en la mesa) and how someone is right now (Estoy bien). ser says what something is (Es un libro) and whose it is (Es de mi mamá). For where a thing is, it's always estar.
ser-estar.why: Ask what you're saying. Where it is, or how someone is: [[está]], [[estoy]]. What it is, or whose: [[es]]. So the same phone is: Es mi teléfono (what it is), and Está en la mesa (where it is).

examples.text: El teléfono está en la mesa.
examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.text: El teléfono es de mi mamá.
examples.literal: The phone is of my mom.

contrasts.says: English uses is for all of these; Spanish chooses between es and está.
Whose something is takes ser and de: es de mi mamá.

mistakes.wrong: El teléfono es en la mesa.
mistakes.right: El teléfono está en la mesa.
mistakes.why: Where a thing is takes estar.
How you are takes estar.
What something is takes ser.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: mi (my) and tu (your, to someone you say tú to) go before the noun, and they're the same for el and la words: mi libro, mi llave, tu carro, tu casa. With a plural noun they add -s: mis llaves. su says his, her, its, their, and your to someone you say usted to.
possessive.why: Where English says my, Spanish puts [[mi]] in place of el or la: el libro becomes [[mi libro]], la llave becomes [[mi llave]]. Written with an accent, mí is a different word: me.

examples.text: Mi teléfono está en mi bolsillo.
examples.means: My phone is in my pocket.
examples.literal: My phone is in my pocket.
That one is of your dad?

contrasts.says: el and la change with the noun; mi and tu don't.
For someone's, Spanish says de: el libro de mi mamá, my mom's book.

mistakes.why: mí with an accent is me; my is mi.
mi takes the place of la; they don't go together.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

negation.explain: no goes right before the verb: No tomo café, Ella no viene, El café no está listo. Answering a question with no, the first no is the answer and the second goes before the verb: No, no tomo leche. There's no word like English do in it.
negation.why: English puts not after a helper (I do not drink); Spanish has no helper, so [[no]] goes straight before the verb: [[No tomo]] café.

contrasts.says: English adds do or does with not; Spanish just puts no before the verb.
A question with no keeps it before the verb too: ¿Tú no tomas café?

mistakes.why: no goes before the verb, not after it.
no goes before está.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

modal.explain: After querer (want), poder (can) and tener que (have to), the next verb stays in its basic form, the one that ends in -ar, -er or -ir: Quiero comer, ¿Puedes leer eso?, Tengo que trabajar. Only the first verb changes for who does it. Nothing goes between them: no a, no to.
modal.why: One verb at a time takes the person's ending. [[Quiero]] already says I want, so the second stays plain: [[Quiero comer]], never quiero como.

examples.means: I want to have a coffee.
examples.literal: I want to have a coffee.

examples.text: Mi mamá quiere comer en casa.
examples.means: My mom wants to eat at home.
examples.literal: My mom wants to eat at home.

contrasts.says: The first verb takes the ending (quiero, quieres, quiere); the second never does.
English puts to between them (want to eat); Spanish puts nothing: quiero comer.

mistakes.why: After quiero, the basic form.
Nothing goes between querer and the next verb.
Have to is tener que, with que.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: esto (this) and eso (that) point at a thing you don't name: ¿Qué es esto?, Eso es un libro. este and ese go with a noun, or stand for one you could name, and match it: este libro, esa mesa, ese (that one). esto and eso never go before a noun.
demonstrative.why: Pointing at something you haven't named yet, use [[esto]] or [[eso]]: ¿Qué es [[eso]]? Once it's a book, it's ese libro, or just [[ese]], that one.

examples.literal: That one is of your dad?

contrasts.says: este and ese match their noun (esta, esa); esto and eso never change.

mistakes.why: Before a noun, este, never esto.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

usted.explain: usted is the polite you, for someone you don't know well, someone older, or anyone you want to show respect to. Its verb takes the form for él and ella: ¿Usted sabe dónde está?, ¿Sabe usted qué es esto? After a word like para it stays usted: Esto es para usted.
usted.why: usted grew out of an old way of saying your grace, so it takes the verb of a third person: [[usted sabe]], like él sabe, never usted sabes.

examples.means: Do you know where my car is?
examples.literal: You know where is my car?

examples.means: Do you know what this is?

contrasts.says: usted is said more often than tú, because sabe alone could also be he or she knows.
usted takes the él and ella ending: usted toma, usted quiere, usted tiene.

mistakes.why: usted takes the él and ella form.
After para, tú becomes ti; usted stays usted.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

de.explain: de joins two nouns where English puts one before the other, and it says whose something is: la llave de mi carro (the key of my car: my car key), el libro de mi mamá (my mom's book), Es de mi mamá (it's my mom's). Spanish has no 's.
de.why: English says my mom's book; Spanish turns it round: el libro [[de]] mi mamá, the book of my mom.

examples.text: El teléfono es de mi mamá.
examples.literal: The phone is of my mom.

examples.text: ¿Él tiene la llave de mi carro?
examples.means: Does he have the key to my car?
examples.literal: He has the key of my car?

examples.text: Entonces voy a casa de mi papá.
examples.means: Then I'll go to my dad's.
examples.literal: Then I go to house of my dad.

contrasts.says: Whose something is takes ser: es de mi mamá.
English uses 's or puts the nouns side by side; Spanish uses de.

mistakes.right: Es el libro de mi mamá.
mistakes.why: Spanish has no 's: the book of my mom.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

hay.explain: hay introduces something present or available. It means there is with one thing and there are with more than one; hay itself does not change. Use it with a new or unspecified person or thing: Hay alguien en la puerta, Hay una puerta abierta. To locate a particular door already being discussed, use estar: La puerta está aquí.
hay.why: Spanish needs no separate word for there: [[Hay]] café is a complete sentence. In [[Hay alguien]] en la puerta, you introduce someone rather than locate a person already named.

examples.literal: There is someone at the door.

contrasts.says: Use hay to introduce what is there; use estar to locate something already identified: El café está aquí.

mistakes.why: puerta is feminine, so use una. hay stays the same.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

adjective-after.explain: A descriptive adjective often follows its noun: una puerta abierta, an open door. It agrees with the noun: abierto with carro, abierta with puerta. Other placements can be grammatical and can change emphasis or meaning; noun first is the useful pattern here.
adjective-after.why: English puts open before door. Spanish puts it after here: una puerta [[abierta]]. The -a matches the feminine noun puerta.

examples.means: I walk to the open door.
examples.literal: I walk to the door open.

contrasts.says: The position and the ending are separate: abierta follows puerta and agrees with it.
In La puerta está abierta, abierta describes a state after estar; it is not part of the noun phrase la puerta abierta.

mistakes.why: abierta agrees with feminine puerta.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question-word.explain: Use qué for what, quién for who, dónde for where and cómo for how. They ask for the missing part of an answer and carry written accents. Spanish does not add do or does. A preposition may come before the question word when the construction needs it. The verb often follows the question word, but this is not a ban on other natural Spanish orders.
question-word.why: In [[¿Cómo]] puedo ayudar?, you are asking how to help. In [[¿Dónde]] está tu amigo?, the missing information is the place.

contrasts.says: A yes-or-no question asks whether something is true; a question word asks for a person, place, thing or other missing information.

mistakes.why: The question word does not change the rule after puedo: use the infinitive ayudar.
The subject tu amigo takes está, not the tú form estás.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

personal-a.explain: With verbs such as ayudar, a specific person as the direct object normally takes a before them: Ayudo a mi amigo. This a does not mean that anyone is moving toward the person. Do not copy it automatically to things or to every verb with a person; learn the verb and its construction.
personal-a.why: In Ayudo [[a mi amigo]], mi amigo is the person receiving the help. English says help my friend without a word for this a.

examples.text: Ayudo a mi amigo con el carro.
examples.means: I'm helping my friend with the car.
examples.literal: I help to my friend with the car.

examples.text: Ayudo a tu mamá en casa.
examples.means: I help your mom at home.
examples.literal: I help to your mom at home.

contrasts.says: Spanish uses personal a in these sentences; English help takes the person directly.
mi and tu still describe whose friend or parent it is; a goes before the whole phrase.

mistakes.why: The subject yo requires ayudo. Personal a does not change the verb ending.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

progressive.explain: Use a form of estar followed by the gerund to present an action in progress: Estoy buscando mi llave. For buscar the gerund is buscando; it does not change for the person or for gender. estar changes: estoy, estás, está, están. Spanish also uses its simple present for many situations where English uses an -ing form.
progressive.why: [[Estoy buscando]] makes the search an action in progress. Change who is searching and only estar changes: [[Estás buscando]].

examples.means: Today I'm looking for my key.
examples.literal: Today I am looking for my key.

examples.means: Are you looking in the car?
examples.literal: Are you looking in the car?
They are looking for the key.

contrasts.says: Ellos vienen hoy uses the simple present for an arranged arrival today; an English -ing does not automatically require the Spanish progressive.
After puedo use buscar; after estoy for an ongoing action use buscando.

mistakes.why: estar must agree with yo.
The plural subject ellos takes están; buscando stays unchanged.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

plural.explain: For common nouns ending in a vowel, add -s: cita becomes citas, hora becomes horas. Many nouns ending in a consonant add -es; a final z changes to c before that ending. The article and describing words agree with the noun, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. Feminine plural nouns take las rather than la.
plural.why: Two appointments are dos [[citas]]. As a subject they take a plural verb: [[Las citas son]] a las dos.

examples.text: Tengo una cita en dos horas.
examples.means: I have an appointment in two hours.
examples.literal: I have an appointment in two hours.

examples.text: Las citas son a las dos.
examples.means: The appointments are at two o'clock.
examples.literal: The appointments are at the two.

contrasts.says: Gender stays the same in the plural: cita and citas are feminine.
hay itself does not become plural: Hay dos citas.

mistakes.why: After dos, use the plural citas.

mistakes.wrong: Las citas es a las dos.
mistakes.right: Las citas son a las dos.
mistakes.why: The plural subject las citas takes son.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

contractions.explain: a and de join the masculine singular article el in ordinary noun phrases: a + el becomes al, de + el becomes del. They do not join la, las or los. The pronoun él, meaning he or him, is different from the article and stays separate. In ver al doctor the a is personal a, joined to the article el.
contractions.why: Keep the personal a and the article, but write them together: ver [[al]] doctor.

examples.means: I want to see the doctor.
examples.literal: I want to see to the doctor.

examples.text: Quiero ver al doctor en una hora.
examples.means: I want to see the doctor in an hour.
examples.literal: I want to see to the doctor in an hour.

contrasts.says: ver al doctor includes personal a before the doctor; ver la puerta has no personal a.
del combines de with el. With mi, keep de separate: la puerta de mi carro.

mistakes.why: a and the article el contract to al.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.explain: To tell the time, use es la una for one o'clock and son las with other hours: Son las dos. To say when something happens, use a la una or a las dos. The feminine articles refer to hours. An appointment remains singular even if its time contains las: Mi cita es a las dos.
time-telling.why: [[Son las dos]] answers what time it is. Mi cita es [[a las dos]] tells when the appointment is. The a makes it at two.

examples.text: Mi cita es a las dos.
examples.means: My appointment is at two o'clock.
examples.literal: My appointment is at the two.

examples.text: A las dos tengo que trabajar.
examples.means: At two o'clock I have to work.
examples.literal: At the two I have to work.

contrasts.says: Use ser to tell the time and to say when an appointment is.
las agrees with the understood plural hours; it does not make mi cita plural.

mistakes.why: Use the plural article las for two o'clock.

mistakes.wrong: Mi cita son a las dos.
mistakes.right: Mi cita es a las dos.
mistakes.why: Here the subject is singular mi cita, so the verb is es.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

prepositional-pronoun.explain: contigo means with you when addressing one person as tú. It is one word, used after the verb or wherever the with-you phrase belongs: Quiero estar contigo. More generally, many prepositions take mí and ti; with con the forms are conmigo and contigo. Pronouns such as él, ella and usted keep their form after a preposition.
prepositional-pronoun.why: The con is already inside [[contigo]]. There is no separate con before it: Quiero estar [[contigo]].

examples.means: I want to be with you.
examples.literal: I want to be with you.

examples.means: I can be with you now.
examples.literal: I can be with you now.

contrasts.says: tú is used as a subject; contigo is the with-you phrase.
To someone you address as usted, use con usted. contigo belongs to tú.

mistakes.why: With con, the familiar singular you is contigo, not tú.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.explain: Use a command form to ask or tell someone to act. With one person you address as tú, llamar gives llama: Llama al doctor, por favor. Many regular affirmative tú commands look like the él or ella present form, but common irregular commands must be learned. A subject word is usually unnecessary. Object pronouns attach to affirmative commands; negative commands use a different form, taught later.
imperative.why: [[Llama]] addresses the listener and asks for action. por favor makes the request polite without changing the familiar tú command.

contrasts.says: llama can also be a present-tense statement about someone else. The situation, subject and intonation distinguish the request.
Adding por favor does not turn a tú command into an usted command; the verb form must change for usted.

mistakes.why: An explicit tú requires the tú command llama, not the usted command llame.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

pronoun-attached.explain: An object pronoun can attach to an infinitive: ayudar plus me becomes ayudarme, to help me. With poder and an infinitive, it can instead go before the conjugated verb: Me puedes ayudar. It does not go between puedes and ayudar. Pronouns also attach to affirmative commands and can attach to gerunds; add a written accent when the spelling rules require it.
pronoun-attached.why: In ¿Puedes [[ayudarme]]?, me is the person receiving the help. The infinitive and its pronoun are written together; English keeps help me as two words.

examples.means: Do you have a moment to help me?
examples.literal: You have a moment for to help me?

contrasts.says: The verb remains an infinitive after puedes: ayudarme contains ayudar, not a conjugated form.
Before a conjugated verb the pronoun is separate; on an infinitive it is attached.

mistakes.why: yo is a subject pronoun. The person helped is me, attached here to ayudar.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

reflexive.explain: Some verbs are learned with a pronoun that matches the subject. quedarse means to stay: me quedo for I stay, te quedas for you stay. The pronoun is required for this use. It does not literally mean that you do an action to yourself; pronominal verbs can have their own meanings. Both the pronoun and the verb form follow the person.
reflexive.why: In [[me quedo]], me goes with the first-person form quedo. In [[te quedas]], te goes with the tú form quedas. Learn each pair together.

examples.text: Esta noche me quedo en casa.
examples.literal: Tonight myself I stay at home.

contrasts.says: The pronoun in quedarse belongs to the verb and refers back to its subject; an ordinary object can refer to another person.
me and te do not replace the ending. The ending still changes for the subject.

mistakes.why: yo requires quedo.
tú requires quedas.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-preposition.explain: Do not copy an English verb's preposition automatically. esperar means wait or wait for: Esperamos al doctor. When the person awaited is specific, personal a comes before that person, and a plus el becomes al. For a length of waiting, use hasta for the endpoint: Esperamos hasta las tres. Other verbs have their own patterns to learn.
verb-preposition.why: English uses wait for the doctor. Spanish uses esperamos [[al doctor]]: that a marks the person as an object; it is not a translation of for.

examples.means: We're waiting here for the doctor.
examples.literal: We wait for here to the doctor.
I wait for to my friend.

contrasts.says: The a before a specific person is personal a.
The a and the article el combine: al doctor. There is no contraction in a mi amiga.

mistakes.why: Personal a combines with the article el.
The verb still agrees with its subject yo.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

object-pronoun.explain: me means me and te means you when that person is the object of a verb: ¿Me oyes?, Te oigo. These little pronouns go before a conjugated verb in ordinary present-tense statements and questions. With no, put no before the pronoun: No te oigo. The verb ending identifies the person hearing; the pronoun identifies the person heard. These same forms can also mark a recipient, depending on the verb.
object-pronoun.why: [[Te]] oigo means I hear you: te is you, and oigo says I hear. [[Me]] oyes reverses the roles: you hear me.

contrasts.says: In me quedo, the pronoun belongs to quedarse and refers to its subject. In me oyes, me is the person that you hear.
With an infinitive, a pronoun can attach to the end: ayudarme. It is separate before oyes or oigo.

mistakes.why: oigo agrees with the subject yo. te is the object, not the subject.
oyes agrees with the subject tú. me is the person heard.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.
